title: verl: the HybridFlow RL training stack for LLMs
summary: How verl runs RL post-training: a single controller drives SPMD WorkerGroups, DataProto moves batches, a GRPO step runs call by call, and the 3D-HybridEngine reshards actor weights.
outcomes: Explain why verl runs the RL loop in one controller process but each model's computation SPMD across GPUs
Trace how @register dispatch modes split a DataProto across a WorkerGroup and gather the results
Compute responses, mini-batches and optimizer steps per RL step from verl's batch-size config
Compute 3D-HybridEngine resharding volume and peak memory from the HybridFlow formulas
Choose between colocated and split placements and the knobs that prevent out-of-memory at transitions

lessons.title: Why verl splits the RL loop from the GPU programs

blocks.md: From the RL infrastructure course you know the shape of one RL step for an LLM: the actor **generates** responses, other models **score** them (reward, reference log-probs, values), then the actor (and critic, if any) **trains**. verl is one concrete system for running that loop. It is the open-source implementation of the **HybridFlow** paper (Sheng et al., EuroSys 2025), started by the ByteDance Seed team and now maintained by the verl community under the `verl-project` GitHub organization.

HybridFlow describes RL as a **dataflow graph**. In classic deep RL a node is a small network that fits in one process. In RL for LLMs every node is itself a **distributed program**: training, inference or generation of a multi-billion-parameter model sharded with tensor, pipeline or data parallelism. Every edge becomes a **many-to-many reshard**, because the producer and consumer models can be split across GPUs in different ways.

There are two classic ways to run such a graph.

- **Single controller**: one central process tells every worker what to do. It has a global view, so changing the algorithm is easy, but dispatching every operation of a sharded LLM from one process is too slow.
- **Multi-controller** (SPMD, as in `torchrun` with Megatron-LM): every GPU runs its own copy of the program. Dispatch is cheap, but the RL loop must be woven into each model's program as explicit send and receive calls, so changing one model's inputs means editing every model that talks to it.

blocks.title: Single, multi and hybrid controllers for one PPO step

scenes.caption: Multi-controller: each model runs its own SPMD program, and the programs coordinate with point-to-point sends. Computation and data movement are nested in the same code.
Pure single controller: one process drives every worker. Easy to change the algorithm, but per-operation dispatch to hundreds of GPUs becomes the bottleneck for LLM-sized models.
Hybrid: the controller issues one call per stage (generate, compute values, ...). Inside each WorkerGroup the work runs SPMD, so kernels never wait on the controller.
Because the loop only names stages, swapping the actor's engine (say FSDP plus vLLM for Megatron-LM plus SGLang) leaves the controller code untouched.

blocks.md: verl's programming guide frames the same split as **control flow** versus **computation flow**. Control flow is the RL algorithm: roll out, compute advantages, train. Computation flow is the neural network work: forward, backward, optimizer step. verl runs the control flow in a single process and the computation flow in many processes, so the training loop reads like a single-process script:

blocks.code:
for prompt in dataloader:
    output = actor_rollout_ref_wg.generate_sequences(prompt)
    old_log_prob = actor_rollout_ref_wg.compute_log_prob(output)
    ref_log_prob = actor_rollout_ref_wg.compute_ref_log_prob(output)
    values = critic_wg.compute_values(output)
    rewards = reward_wg.compute_scores(output)
    # runs on the controller process itself
    advantages = compute_advantages(values, rewards)
    output = output.union(old_log_prob).union(ref_log_prob)
    output = output.union(values).union(rewards).union(advantages)
    actor_rollout_ref_wg.update_actor(output)
    critic_wg.update_critic(output)
blocks.caption: The PPO loop as written in verl's HybridFlow programming guide (lightly condensed). Each call on a WorkerGroup fans out to many GPU processes.

blocks.md: The controller decides **what runs and in what order**; each WorkerGroup decides **how** it runs on its GPUs. That is why a new algorithm is a change to one Python loop, and a new backend or placement is a change to the workers or the config, never both.

The split is not free. verl's docs list the cost: data must travel between the controller and the worker processes at every stage. The driver (the Ray task that runs the trainer's `fit`, called `main_task` in the docs) holds whole batches in the classic trainer, so the docs recommend not scheduling it on the Ray head node, which usually has few resources.

blocks.question: A researcher wants to add a second, greedy generation pass per prompt (as ReMax does) to compute a baseline. In verl's design, what has to change?
options: Every worker's SPMD program, because each must know when the extra pass happens
Only the controller loop: one more call to the existing generate_sequences with sampling turned off
The NCCL communicator setup between actor and critic
Nothing: verl decides which passes to run from the model architecture
blocks.explain: Stages are named calls on WorkerGroups, so a new dataflow is a new sequence of calls in the controller. The HybridFlow paper shows PPO, ReMax and Safe-RLHF differing only in these few lines. In a multi-controller design the extra pass would have to be threaded through every model's program.

blocks.question: Why doesn't HybridFlow simply use a single controller for everything, as classic RL frameworks such as RLlib do?
options: Single controllers cannot express data dependencies between models
Ray does not support GPU workers
Dispatching every operation of a sharded LLM from one central process adds too much overhead; SPMD inside each model avoids it
A single controller forces all models to use the same parallelism
blocks.explain: The paper's diagnosis: single-controller frameworks were built for networks of at most hundreds of MB. For LLMs with complex parallelism the central dispatch overhead is too high, so HybridFlow keeps central control only between nodes and lets each node run multi-controller.

lessons.title: WorkerGroups, resource pools and DataProto dispatch

blocks.md:
verl builds the controller side on **Ray**, which can expose a Python class's methods as remote calls. Three pieces turn Ray's one-call-one-process model into one call that fans out to many GPUs:

- A **Worker** is a Ray actor process bound to one GPU. It owns a model shard and exposes methods such as `init_model`, `compute_log_prob`, `compute_ref_log_prob` and `update_actor`.
- A **ResourcePool** is a set of GPUs, described as processes per node, for example `[8] * nnodes`.
- A **RayWorkerGroup** launches one Worker per GPU in a pool and acts as a proxy: calling a method on the group calls it on every worker.

Placement is just a mapping. A `ResourcePoolManager` maps each role (actor and rollout, critic, reference, reward model) to a named pool. Roles on the **same** pool are colocated on the same GPUs; roles on **different** pools run on disjoint GPUs. For colocated roles, `create_colocated_worker_cls` fuses several role classes into one Ray actor per GPU, which saves the redundant CUDA and distributed contexts that separate processes would create.

In PPO the biggest fused role is **ActorRolloutRef**: actor training, rollout generation and the reference policy in one worker class. The docs give two reasons: actor and rollout share GPUs so new weights move fast, and with LoRA the reference policy is simply the base model, so it can live in the same process.

How does one call become many? A worker method is decorated with `@register(dispatch_mode=...)`. The decorator only attaches metadata. When the WorkerGroup is built, `_bind_worker_method` reads it and generates a group-level method from three functions: a **dispatch_fn** that splits the arguments per worker, an **execute_fn** that calls every worker remotely, and a **collect_fn** that merges the results.

blocks.title: One call to generate_sequences with DP_COMPUTE_PROTO

scenes.caption: The controller calls the method once, as in a single-process script, passing one DataProto with 4 prompts. This is the docs' example; current workers generate via the agent loop and use the N-D dispatch below.
dispatch_fn for DP_COMPUTE_PROTO calls DataProto.chunk to split the batch into world_size pieces, one per worker.
execute_fn (execute_all) invokes the method remotely on every worker. Each worker runs its SPMD program on its own chunk.
collect_fn concatenates the outputs back into one DataProto, so the controller sees a single result in the original order.

blocks.md:
The unit of exchange is **DataProto** (`verl/protocol.py`). It has three fields:

- `batch`: a `TensorDict` of tensors that share the first (batch) dimension, such as `input_ids`, `responses`, `old_log_probs`, `advantages`.
- `non_tensor_batch`: a dict of NumPy arrays with the same length, such as `uid`, `data_source` or ground-truth strings.
- `meta_info`: a plain dict for per-batch facts such as metrics or `global_token_num`.

The controller builds a step's batch by repeatedly calling `union`, which merges keys and raises an error on conflicting values or mismatched batch sizes.

blocks.prompt: The controller sends a DataProto of 10 samples to a WorkerGroup of 4 workers with DP_COMPUTE_PROTO and auto-padding enabled. How many samples does each worker get, and what does the controller get back?
blocks.reveal: Each worker gets **3** samples. 10 is not divisible by 4, so the dispatcher pads with $4 - (10 \bmod 4) = 2$ copies of the last sample, giving 12. After collecting, the generated method drops the last 2 outputs, so the controller gets back exactly 10 results. Without padding enabled, `DataProto.chunk` asserts that the length divides evenly and fails.

blocks.title: Auto-padding before a DP split (simplified from decorator.py)
blocks.code:
def dispatch(batch, world_size):
    n = len(batch)
    rem = n % world_size
    pad = (world_size - rem) if rem > 0 else 0
    batch = batch + [batch[-1]] * pad
    size = len(batch) // world_size
    chunks = [batch[i*size:(i+1)*size]
              for i in range(world_size)]
    return chunks, pad

def collect(outputs, pad):
    merged = sum(outputs, [])
    return merged[:len(merged) - pad]

scenes.caption: 10 samples arrive for 4 workers.
10 mod 4 is 2, so 2 padding samples are needed to make equal chunks.
Padding repeats the last sample (the real code selects index len-1 by default).
Each worker gets 3 samples.
After execution, the padded tail is dropped so the controller sees 10 results.

blocks.md: Plain data parallelism is not enough when a worker group also uses tensor or pipeline parallelism, because GPUs in the same tensor-parallel group must see the **same** data. verl's engine workers therefore use `make_nd_compute_dataproto_dispatch_fn(mesh_name)`. Each worker registers its **data-parallel rank** and whether it is a **collect rank**. The batch is split into as many chunks as there are DP ranks, each worker receives its DP rank's chunk, and outputs are gathered only from collect ranks. For the Megatron engine a collect rank is tensor-parallel rank 0 on the last pipeline stage (and context-parallel rank 0).

blocks.title: Dispatch on 8 GPUs with tensor parallel size 2

scenes.caption: 8 workers, TP size 2, so ranks pair up into 4 tensor-parallel groups. The batch must be split by DP rank, not by global rank.
dp_rank_mapping is [0,0,1,1,2,2,3,3]: the controller makes 4 chunks and both members of a TP pair receive the same chunk.
Both TP ranks compute the same logical output, so only TP rank 0 of each pair is collected. 4 outputs come back and are concatenated in DP order.

blocks.md: Do not read `world_size` as the data-parallel size. On 8 GPUs with TP 2 a WorkerGroup has 8 workers but only 4 data shards. Splitting the batch 8 ways would hand different samples to two GPUs that must run the same sharded matmul together.

blocks.question: `init_model` is registered with Dispatch.ONE_TO_ALL. What does the controller send to each worker when it calls `wg.init_model()`?
options: A different slice of the arguments to each worker
The same arguments, replicated once per worker
Arguments only to rank 0, which then broadcasts them
Nothing; ONE_TO_ALL methods run on the controller process
blocks.explain: dispatch_one_to_all copies every argument world_size times, so every worker runs the same call. It suits setup methods like init_model. DP_COMPUTE_PROTO is the mode that splits a DataProto into per-worker chunks.

blocks.question: Two roles are mapped to the same ResourcePool and fused with create_colocated_worker_cls. What is the main effect?
options: Both roles run in one Ray actor per GPU and share one CUDA and distributed context
Both roles get disjoint halves of the pool's GPUs
The roles run concurrently on the GPU with separate memory pools
The roles are forced to use the same model weights
blocks.explain: Same pool means same GPUs; fusing the classes avoids one process per role per GPU. The roles still run one after another in the order the controller calls them. Disjoint GPUs require different pools.

lessons.title: One GRPO step through RayPPOTrainer, call by call

blocks.md: Training starts with `python3 -m verl.trainer.main_ppo` plus Hydra overrides. The entry point starts a trainer whose `fit()` method is the single controller: it runs as one process and calls the WorkerGroups. On current main the default (`trainer.use_v1=true`) is the V1 `PPOTrainerSync`, which keeps batch tensors in a TransferQueue and hands workers keys; this lesson follows the classic `RayPPOTrainer` in `ray_trainer.py` (now deprecated), which runs the same stages with DataProto. PPO and GRPO share this trainer; GRPO is mostly configuration. The official GRPO example for Qwen3-8B on 8 GPUs sets, among others:

blocks.code:
python3 -m verl.trainer.main_ppo \
  algorithm.adv_estimator=grpo \
  algorithm.use_kl_in_reward=False \
  data.train_batch_size=1024 \
  data.max_prompt_length=1024 \
  data.max_response_length=2048 \
  actor_rollout_ref.model.path=Qwen/Qwen3-8B \
  actor_rollout_ref.actor.optim.lr=1e-6 \
  actor_rollout_ref.actor.ppo_mini_batch_size=256 \
  actor_rollout_ref.actor.use_kl_loss=True \
  actor_rollout_ref.actor.kl_loss_coef=0.001 \
  actor_rollout_ref.actor.kl_loss_type=low_var_kl \
  actor_rollout_ref.rollout.name=vllm \
  actor_rollout_ref.rollout.tensor_model_parallel_size=2 \
  actor_rollout_ref.rollout.gpu_memory_utilization=0.6 \
  actor_rollout_ref.rollout.n=5 \
  trainer.n_gpus_per_node=8 trainer.nnodes=1
blocks.caption: Selected overrides from examples/grpo_trainer/run_qwen3_8b_fsdp.sh (GPU defaults). The config tree has top-level groups data, actor_rollout_ref (model, actor, rollout, ref), critic, reward, algorithm and trainer.

blocks.md: Batch sizes are counted in **prompts**. `data.train_batch_size=1024` with `rollout.n=5` yields $1024 \times 5 = 5120$ responses per step. `ppo_mini_batch_size=256` is also in prompts: the trainer multiplies it by `n`, so each optimizer step sees $256 \times 5 = 1280$ responses, and with `ppo_epochs=1` the actor takes $5120 / 1280 = 4$ optimizer steps per RL step. Micro-batch settings (`ppo_micro_batch_size_per_gpu`, or `use_dynamic_bsz` with `ppo_max_token_len_per_gpu`) only cap memory per forward pass; the GRPO docs note they should not change the algorithm.

blocks.title: Order of work in one synchronous GRPO step

scenes.caption: Schematic durations, not measurements. The controller repeats each prompt n times and asks the agent loop manager to generate; vLLM or SGLang servers on the same GPUs serve the requests.
With rule-based rewards, the reward loop scores each sample as soon as it finishes rolling out. When generation ends, the rollout replicas sleep: KV cache and weights leave GPU memory.
The actor recomputes old log-probs under its training engine, then the reference model computes reference log-probs for the KL loss. Both are forward passes only.
compute_advantage runs on the controller itself: cheap arithmetic over the gathered batch, grouped by each prompt's uid.
update_actor runs the 4 mini-batch optimizer steps computed above on the training engine (FSDP or Megatron).
update_weights wakes the rollout's weight memory, streams the new actor parameters into it, and only then restores the KV cache, ready for the next step.

blocks.md: Rollout goes through the **agent loop**. The trainer calls `AgentLoopManager.generate_sequences`; the manager splits the batch into chunks for `AgentLoopWorker`s, each worker runs one `AgentLoopBase.run` coroutine per prompt, and generation requests go to vLLM or SGLang **server** instances, choosing the server with the fewest requests on the first turn and sticking to it for later turns. A single-turn prompt is just the simplest agent loop; multi-turn tool use plugs into the same interface.

Rewards come from the **reward loop**, verl's default reward path. `reward.num_workers` (default 8) reward workers score chunks in parallel, and with rule-based rewards scoring streams alongside rollout. A custom rule is a plain Python function, pointed to by `reward.custom_reward_function.path` and `.name` (default name `compute_score`):

blocks.code:
# my_reward.py
def compute_score(data_source, solution_str, ground_truth, extra_info=None):
    # 1.0 if the last line contains the reference answer, else 0.0
    last = solution_str.strip().splitlines()[-1] if solution_str.strip() else ""
    return 1.0 if ground_truth in last else 0.0
blocks.caption: The documented signature for a custom reward function. data_source and ground_truth come from the dataset's parquet columns via non_tensor_batch.

blocks.md: Before training, each prompt gets a unique `uid` in `non_tensor_batch`, and `repeat(n, interleave=True)` places the n copies of a prompt next to each other. `compute_grpo_outcome_advantage` sums each response's token rewards into one score, groups scores by `uid`, and computes $(r - \text{mean}) / (\text{std} + 10^{-6})$ with PyTorch's sample standard deviation (or only $r - \text{mean}$ when `norm_adv_by_std_in_grpo=False`, the Dr. GRPO setting).

scenes.caption: Two prompts enter the step, each tagged with a uid.
repeat(5, interleave=True) puts each prompt's 5 copies side by side; the rollout fills in 10 responses.
Rule-based rewards: p0 gets 2 of 5 right; p1 gets all 5 right.
p0: mean 0.4, sample std 0.548, so correct answers get 1.095 and wrong ones -0.730. p1: every reward equals the mean, so all 5 advantages are 0 and the group gives no gradient.

blocks.prompt: With trainer.balance_batch=True, the controller reorders the batch so every DP rank gets a similar number of tokens. Does this reordering scramble GRPO's groups?
blocks.reveal: No. The source comments say it: reordering changes which samples land in which mini-batch, but advantages are grouped by `uid`, not by position, so each response still gets its own group's mean and std. What reordering can change is mini-batch composition, which affects the loss computation, not the advantages.

blocks.md: Read the source, not just the prose. The reward-function doc says the GSM8K scorer gives 0.1 for a well-formatted wrong answer, but in the current `gsm8k.py` the default `format_score` is 0.0. A silent difference like that changes what the policy is rewarded for.

Old log-probs are recomputed by the training engine by default, because the inference engine's numbers can differ slightly. `algorithm.rollout_correction` offers a **bypass mode** that uses the rollout's own log-probs instead, plus importance-sampling weights and rejection sampling to correct the mismatch.

blocks.question: data.train_batch_size=512, rollout.n=8, actor.ppo_mini_batch_size=128, ppo_epochs=1. How many actor optimizer steps happen per RL step?
blocks.explain: 512 prompts x 8 = 4096 responses. The mini-batch is 128 prompts, which the trainer scales to 128 x 8 = 1024 responses. 4096 / 1024 = 4 optimizer steps. Reading ppo_mini_batch_size as responses would give 32, the common mistake.

blocks.question: You halve actor.ppo_micro_batch_size_per_gpu to fix an out-of-memory error. What happens to the learning dynamics?
options: Nothing in principle: micro-batches only split each mini-batch into smaller forward and backward passes with gradient accumulation
Each optimizer step now sees half as many responses
The number of optimizer steps per RL step doubles
GRPO groups get split across micro-batches, which corrupts the advantages
blocks.explain: Micro-batching is like gradient accumulation: it trades speed for memory. The mini-batch size, which sets samples per optimizer step, is unchanged. Advantages were already computed on the controller before update_actor, so splitting groups across micro-batches does not affect them.

lessons.title: 3D-HybridEngine: resharding the actor with zero redundancy

blocks.md: The actor does two very different jobs. **Training** needs gradients and optimizer states, so it uses large model-parallel groups to fit. **Generation** holds only weights and KV cache, and the paper found it usually runs best with smaller tensor-parallel (TP) and pipeline groups and more data-parallel replicas. The HybridFlow paper measured this on 16 GPUs with training groups 1-8-2: a generation TP of 2 cut 7B generation latency by 60.3%, and keeping training's TP of 8 gave the worst latency.

So the same weights must live in two layouts. Keeping two full copies on separate GPUs wastes memory and needs a weight sync every step. HybridFlow instead runs both stages on the **same** $N_a$ GPUs and reshards between them. Notation: training uses $p$-$t$-$d$ (pipeline, tensor, data parallel sizes). Generation uses $p_g$-$t_g$-$d_g$-$d$, where each training replica splits into $d_g$ **micro data-parallel** replicas.

blocks.tex: N_a = p \cdot t \cdot d = p_g \cdot t_g \cdot d_g \cdot d \quad\Rightarrow\quad d_g = \frac{p\,t}{p_g\,t_g}
blocks.caption: The GPU count is fixed, so shrinking the generation model-parallel size multiplies the number of generation replicas.

blocks.md: Consider the paper's Figure 8 example: 8 GPUs, a model cut into quarters q1 to q4. Training uses 1-4-2, so TP groups are [G1..G4] and [G5..G8] and each GPU holds one quarter. Generation uses 1-2-2-2, so each GPU must hold a **half**: q1+q2 or q3+q4. The usual way to build groups is consecutive ranks for TP, so the generation TP groups would be [G1,G2], [G3,G4], and so on.

scenes.caption: Training 1-4-2: each GPU holds one quarter of the weights; [G1..G4] and [G5..G8] are the two data-parallel replicas.
Naive 1-2-2-2 generation: consecutive TP pairs. Rank 0 of each pair takes q1+q2, rank 1 takes q3+q4.
G2, G3, G6 and G7 must hold a half that does not contain their training quarter, so they keep that quarter too: redundant memory. Gathering also spans whole TP groups.

blocks.prompt: You may choose which GPUs form each generation TP group. How could you arrange the groups so that every GPU's generation half contains its own training quarter?
blocks.reveal: Pick generation TP groups by **stride** instead of consecutively: $t / t_g = 2$, so the groups are [G1,G3], [G2,G4], [G5,G7], [G6,G8]. Then G1 and G2 both hold q1+q2 and G3 and G4 both hold q3+q4. The pairs [G1,G2], [G3,G4], ... become the **micro DP groups**, and one all-gather inside each pair builds the half from two quarters already in place.

blocks.title: HybridFlow's grouping: strided TP, consecutive micro DP

scenes.caption: Same training layout as before.
Micro DP groups are consecutive pairs [G1,G2], [G3,G4], [G5,G6], [G7,G8]. Each pair all-gathers its two quarters; all four gathers run at the same time.
Every generation shard contains its GPU's training shard, so training weights are reused in place: zero redundancy. Generation TP groups are [G1,G3], [G2,G4], [G5,G7], [G6,G8].

blocks.md: The paper's Table 2 compares the transition cost for an actor of size $M$ bytes. **DeepSpeed-Chat** all-gathers across all $N_a$ GPUs. **HybridFlow-V** (the naive grouping) all-gathers within training TP and PP groups. Both first materialize the whole model on each GPU, so their peak parameter memory is $M$. **HybridFlow** gathers only inside micro DP groups.

blocks.caption: Communication volume per transition. Peak parameter memory is M, M and M/(t_g p_g); redundant memory is M/(tpd), M/(tp) and 0.

blocks.md: Worked example, using the paper's Figure 15 layout: a 7B actor in bf16 (simplified as $7 \times 10^9 \times 2$ bytes $= 14$ GB), 16 GPUs, training 1-8-2, generation $t_g = 2$, $p_g = 1$, so $d_g = 8/2 = 4$. The training shard is $14/8 = 1.75$ GB and the generation shard is $14/2 = 7$ GB. HybridFlow's volume is $\frac{8-2}{2 \cdot 8} \times 14 = 5.25$ GB, against $\frac{15}{16} \times 14 = 13.125$ GB for DeepSpeed-Chat and $\frac{7}{8} \times 14 = 12.25$ GB for HybridFlow-V.

blocks.title: Transition cost per GPU: 7B actor, 16 GPUs, train 1-8-2, gen TP 2

scenes.caption: Communication volume from Table 2's formulas: HybridFlow moves 5.25 GB versus 12.25 and 13.125 GB, because each all-gather spans only a micro DP group of 4.
Peak parameter memory: the baselines materialize all 14 GB; HybridFlow peaks at the 7 GB generation shard.
Redundant memory held for the next training stage: 0.875 GB (M/16), 1.75 GB (M/8) and zero. Simplified: counts parameters only, not KV cache or activations.

blocks.title: HybridFlow transition volume as generation TP shrinks

scenes.caption: Defaults match the worked example. With t_g = t = 8 nothing is gathered at all, but generation runs with training's large TP, which the paper found slowest.
Smaller t_g means more generation replicas (faster decoding) but a larger gather and a larger per-GPU shard: M/t_g. That leaves less room for KV cache, the paper's reason smaller t_g stops helping.
With training TP 4 the curves shift left: at t_g = 2 the gather is (4-2)/(2x4) of M = 3.5 GB.

blocks.md: In the paper's experiments this cut the training-to-generation transition time by 55.2% (11.7 s) on average and by up to 89.1% (78.2 s) for 70B models, with overhead staying flat as the cluster grew.

The paper describes the mechanism; today's code path is different in detail. With `actor_rollout_ref.hybrid_engine: true`, verl colocates actor and rollout, and the rollout is a vLLM or SGLang server with its own TP. After generation it sleeps (frees KV cache and weights); `update_weights` then wakes the weight memory, streams parameters tensor by tensor from the training engine, and finally restores the KV cache.

Remember the condition that makes resharding free: choose generation groups so that **each GPU's generation shard contains its training shard**. Then the only traffic is one all-gather per micro DP group, and no GPU keeps a second copy.

blocks.question: Training uses p-t-d = 1-4-4 on 16 GPUs and generation uses t_g = 1, p_g = 1. What is d_g, and what does HybridFlow's peak parameter memory per GPU become?
options: d_g = 4; peak M, the whole model on every GPU
d_g = 1; peak M/4
d_g = 16; peak M/16
d_g = 4; peak M/4
blocks.explain: d_g = p t / (p_g t_g) = 4 / 1 = 4. Peak parameter memory is M / (t_g p_g) = M: with no generation model parallelism, every GPU needs the full weights. Zero redundancy does not mean small memory; it means no second copy.

blocks.question: In the naive grouping on 8 GPUs (train 1-4-2, gen 1-2-2-2), why must G2 keep extra memory after the transition?
options: G2 is a pipeline boundary and must buffer activations
Its generation half (q3+q4) does not contain its training quarter (q2), so q2 must be kept for the next training stage
G2 hosts the controller
Consecutive grouping doubles the KV cache on even ranks
blocks.explain: Under consecutive TP grouping, G2 is rank 1 of [G1,G2] and gets q3+q4. Its training shard q2 is not inside that, so it must be stored separately until training resumes. The paper marks G2, G3, G6 and G7 as the GPUs with this redundancy.

lessons.title: Backends, placement and running verl in practice

blocks.md:
verl separates the **training engine** from the **rollout engine**, and you choose each in config.

- Training: the default `model_engine: dp` uses PyTorch FSDP (`actor.strategy` is `fsdp` or `fsdp2`). `model_engine=megatron` switches the actor, reference and critic to Megatron-LM, set with fields such as `actor_rollout_ref.actor.megatron.tensor_model_parallel_size` and `pipeline_model_parallel_size`. The repo also ships torchtitan and VeOmni engines.
- Rollout: `actor_rollout_ref.rollout.name` picks the inference engine, such as `vllm` or `sglang`, with its own `tensor_model_parallel_size`.

The README pitches Megatron for scale: its news section reports the Megatron backend running large MoE models such as DeepSeek-671B and Qwen3-235B. The GRPO examples reflect the split: the Qwen3-8B FSDP script uses rollout TP 2, while the Qwen3-8B Megatron script defaults to actor TP 2 and PP 2 with rollout TP 2. Training and rollout parallelism are configured independently, which is exactly the freedom lesson 4 was about.

blocks.title: Placement: colocated versus split resource pools

scenes.caption: Default (hybrid_engine: true): every role shares one pool and the stages time-share the GPUs. This is DeepSpeed-Chat's placement in the paper's taxonomy.
The paper counts every way to group PPO's 4 models into colocated sets: the Bell number B4 = 15 placements, from all-colocated to all-separate (OpenRLHF's choice).

Async modes give rollout its own GPUs: the V1 trainer's separate_async mode, or the one-step-off and fully async recipes in verl.experimental (hybrid_engine=False plus a rollout pool). New weights reach the rollout servers over NCCL.

blocks.md: Why split at all? In synchronous training the update must wait for the **longest** response. verl's one-step-off doc reports that in DAPO 32B training, rollout took about 70% of total time, and adding GPUs did not shorten it. The one-step-off trainer generates batch $k+1$ while training on batch $k$, so samples are produced by weights one step old: a deliberate, bounded staleness.

scenes.caption: Schematic, using the 70/30 rollout-to-train split from the DAPO 32B note. Colocated: generate, then train, strictly alternating on the same GPUs.

One-step-off: rollout GPUs start batch 2 while trainer GPUs train on batch 1. Batch 2 used pre-update weights, so it is one step stale. Durations are reused only for illustration; real phase times depend on how the GPUs are split.

blocks.md: The paper reported large end-to-end gains from the whole design (hybrid controller, 3D-HybridEngine and auto-mapping) over the RLHF systems of its time, measured on PPO across 7B to 70B models.

blocks.title: HybridFlow PPO throughput speedups reported in the paper

scenes.caption: Average speedups for PPO: 3.67x, 3.25x and 12.52x. NeMo-Aligner's gap came mainly from generation without a KV cache, up to 81.2% of its iteration time.
Best cases: up to 7.84x, 5.93x and 20.57x. These are 2024 baselines; all of these systems have changed since, so treat the numbers as evidence for the design, not a current ranking.

blocks.md:
Knobs that most often decide whether a run fits and how fast it goes, as the config docs describe them:

- `rollout.gpu_memory_utilization`: for vLLM, the fraction of **total** GPU memory the engine may use; for SGLang, its `mem_fraction_static`. Too high starves the colocated training engine.
- `rollout.free_cache_engine` (default True): offload the KV cache after generation.
- `actor.fsdp_config.param_offload` and `optimizer_offload`: trade speed for GPU memory. The docs recommend offloading the reference model for models larger than 7B.
- `actor.use_dynamic_bsz` with `ppo_max_token_len_per_gpu`: pack micro-batches by token count instead of sample count.

Colocation means **time-sharing**, not free memory. Training states, rollout weights and KV cache take turns on the same GPUs, and sleep and wake are what make the turns possible. A rollout that sets `gpu_memory_utilization` as if it owned the GPU, or a training engine that never offloads, will run out of memory at the transition, not inside either stage.

verl in one sentence: a single Python controller expresses the RL algorithm as calls on WorkerGroups; each WorkerGroup runs a training or inference engine SPMD on a resource pool; DataProto carries the batch between them; and actor and rollout share GPUs by resharding or sleeping instead of keeping two copies.

blocks.question: Your synchronous run's step time is dominated by a few very long responses, and the GPUs idle while waiting for them. Which verl option targets exactly this, and what does it cost?
options: Raise ppo_mini_batch_size; it costs more memory
Switch model_engine to megatron; it costs a checkpoint conversion
Lower rollout.n; it costs nothing
Use the one-step-off (or fully async) trainer with a separate rollout pool; training then uses samples from weights one step old
blocks.explain: The async trainers overlap generation with training on separate GPUs, so long-tail generation no longer stalls the update. The price is bounded staleness: data comes from the previous weights. Lowering n changes the algorithm, and mini-batch or engine changes do not touch the rollout tail.

blocks.question: A colocated run trains fine but crashes with out-of-memory right when the first rollout starts after an update. Which setting is the most likely culprit?
options: rollout.gpu_memory_utilization is set too high for GPUs that also hold training state
data.train_batch_size is not divisible by the number of GPUs
algorithm.adv_estimator is set to grpo
trainer.balance_batch is enabled
blocks.explain: At the transition the rollout reclaims its weight and KV cache memory on GPUs where the training engine may still hold parameters or optimizer state. For vLLM, gpu_memory_utilization is a fraction of total memory, so a value that ignores the colocated trainer overcommits. Lowering it or enabling offload addresses the transition.
